Here's the rub. If the resulting algorithm ends up publicly licenced, the developers cannot claim that they were engaged in a defacto employment relationship with the company and it would be legal. Likewise, with public licences, anyone could use the resulting code. However, if they attempt to patent or copyright the resulting algorithms for private use, then the developers are engaged in a de-facto employment relationship and are a.) entitled to be paid a fair market value for their work and can sue for the difference in value and b.) the companies will likely run afoul of all kinds of other employment and contract laws... resulting in a legal quagmire... SEC investigations, probably a major tax audit and other nasty shit.

It's far more likely that they are using this "competition" to vet the abilities of the developers... and will employ them formally to implement the system at a later time to satisfy the aforementioned legal requirements. It's not great but it's not exactly what OP is claiming either.

Schooling system in germany is a little different compared to america and canada. Elementary school every goes to the same school. Grade 1 to grade 4. then students get divided by how skilled and smart they are. Dumb kids go on to "Hauptschule", normal kids go to "Realschule" and the smartypants go on to "Gymnasium".
Graduate after grade 10 from Hauptschule and Realschule you go on to an apprenticeship of your choice. Pretty much every profession in germany has an apprenticeship program. If a student went to Realschule and their grades are high enough they can ad two more years at a technical school or business school. And then if they so choose go take an apprenticeship or go on to university.
The smarty pants at Gymnasium can either graduate at after grade 10 and go to an apprenticeship, or graduate after grade 12 and then go to university.
College doesn't really exist in germany. But completing an apprenticeship is seen as equivalent as a collage education in america and canada.
